name: Blue Moon Cocktail
description: Gin, dry vermouth and crème de violette — pale lilac, floral and the reason violette came back into production.
funFact: Crème de violette vanished from the American market for most of the twentieth century, and the drinks that needed it — Blue Moon, Aviation — were unmakeable until it returned in 2007.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve very cold — the floral note fades as it warms.

name: Bronx Terrace
description: The Bronx with the orange juice swapped for lime and the sweet vermouth dropped. Drier, sharper and largely forgotten.
funFact: It appears in the Savoy directly after the Bronx itself, which is how the book handles variations — no cross-reference, just the next entry along.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime twist or a cherry.
Serve cold.

name: Clover Leaf
description: The Clover Club with a mint leaf on the foam. One garnish separates the two, and the mint changes the whole nose.
funFact: The only difference from a Clover Club is the mint leaf floated on the foam — an unusually small distinction to earn a separate name, and both appear in the same books.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 15 seconds.
Add ice and shake hard again for 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Float a single mint leaf on the foam.

name: Dempsey
description: Gin and calvados with grenadine and absinthe — named for the heavyweight champion, and it hits about as hard.
funFact: Jack Dempsey held the world heavyweight title from 1919 to 1926, exactly the window in which London bartenders were naming drinks after American celebrities.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top.
Serve very cold.

name: Knickerbocker
description: Rum, raspberry, curaçao and lime over crushed ice — a mid-nineteenth-century drink that predates most of the canon.
funFact: Jerry Thomas printed it in 1862, which makes it older than the Manhattan, the Martini and almost everything else still ordered by name.

steps: Shake all ingredients with ice for 10 seconds.
Strain over crushed ice in a goblet.
Garnish with berries and a slice of orange.
Serve with a straw.

name: Merry Widow
description: Gin and dry vermouth in equal parts with Bénédictine, absinthe and bitters. Low-proof by Savoy standards and unusually aromatic.
funFact: At least six unrelated drinks carry the name Merry Widow, after the operetta that was the biggest theatrical hit of the 1900s — bartenders named drinks after whatever was selling tickets.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Old Etonian
description: Gin, Lillet, orange bitters and crème de noyaux — almond and quinine, and about as English as a drink name gets.
funFact: Crème de noyaux is made from apricot and peach kernels rather than almonds, which is why it tastes of marzipan without containing any.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the top and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Opera
description: Gin, Dubonnet and maraschino with orange bitters. Bittersweet, cherry-scented and considerably drier than Dubonnet suggests.
funFact: Dubonnet was created in 1846 to make quinine palatable to French Foreign Legionnaires in North Africa — the same problem that produced tonic water.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Serve cold.

name: Orange Blossom
description: Gin and orange juice, sweetened. A Prohibition drink whose whole job was hiding what the gin tasted like.
funFact: Bathtub gin was frequently undrinkable, and the Orange Blossom exists as a solution to that problem — which is why it fell out of favour the moment good gin was legal again.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with an orange twist.
Serve very cold.

name: Poet's Dream
description: Gin, dry vermouth and Bénédictine with a lemon twist. Three ingredients, and the Bénédictine does all the talking.
funFact: Bénédictine's label carries the letters D.O.M. — Deo Optimo Maximo, 'to God, most good, most great' — a monastic dedication that survived the liqueur going fully commercial in 1863.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the top and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Red Snapper
description: The Bloody Mary's gin original. Fernand Petiot rebuilt it with gin at the St. Regis, and the name was a euphemism.
funFact: Petiot brought the drink from Harry's Bar in Paris to the St. Regis in New York, where management thought 'Bloody Mary' too coarse for the King Cole Bar — so it became the Red Snapper.

steps: Combine everything in a shaker with ice.
Roll the drink between two tins rather than shaking, so it does not froth.
Strain into a highball glass over fresh ice.
Garnish with a celery stalk and a lemon wedge.
Season further at the table.

name: Royal Bermuda Yacht Club
description: Rum, lime, falernum and curaçao — the club's own drink, and a sharper alternative to its Rum Swizzle.
funFact: The Royal Bermuda Yacht Club received its royal warrant in 1845 from Prince Albert, and the drink named for it appears in Trader Vic's book a century later.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
Serve immediately.

name: Seventh Heaven
description: Gin, maraschino and grapefruit with a mint sprig. Bright, cherry-scented and one of the Savoy's better short sours.
funFact: The Savoy Cocktail Book contains roughly 750 recipes, most of them gin, and the ones that survived are almost all the ones with fresh citrus in them.

steps: Shake the gin, maraschino and grapefruit juice hard with ice.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Slap a mint sprig between your palms and float it on top.
Serve very cold.

name: Tipperary
description: Irish whiskey, sweet vermouth and green Chartreuse in equal parts. Herbal, sweet and much heavier than the name suggests.
funFact: Named for the marching song rather than the county; 'It's a Long Way to Tipperary' was written in 1912 and became the defining British song of the First World War.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface.
Modern versions cut the Chartreuse back; the equal-parts original is the historic one.

name: Waldorf
description: A Manhattan rinsed with absinthe. The hotel that gave us the Bronx and the Rob Roy produced this too.
funFact: The original Waldorf-Astoria stood where the Empire State Building now is; its bar produced a remarkable share of the American canon before it was demolished in 1929.

steps: Rinse a chilled coupe with absinthe and discard the excess.
Stir the rye, vermouth and bitters over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into the rinsed coupe.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.

name: Yale
description: A Martini turned blue with a dash of crème de violette, and stiffened with orange bitters.
funFact: American universities each acquired a cocktail in the early 1900s — Yale, Princeton, Harvard — in a fashion that says more about who was drinking in hotel bars than about the colleges.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a thoroughly chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve very cold.

name: Fallen Angel
description: Gin, lime and crème de menthe with bitters. Mint and juniper together, which sounds wrong and drinks clean.
funFact: White crème de menthe is the same liqueur as the green one without the colouring, which is why a Fallen Angel looks like a Gimlet and tastes nothing like one.

steps: Shake all ingredients hard with ice for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a mint leaf.
Serve very cold.

name: Napoleon
description: Gin with three dashes each of Dubonnet, curaçao and Fernet. Almost neat gin, seasoned rather than mixed.
funFact: Fernet in dashes rather than measures is a nineteenth-century habit that modern bartenders rediscovered — a quarter-teaspoon changes a drink that an ounce would destroy.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 30 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express a lemon twist over the surface and discard it.
Serve extremely cold.

name: Wassail
description: Hot spiced ale with roasted apples bobbing in it, carried house to house at midwinter. Older than the word cocktail by centuries.
funFact: 'Wassail' comes from the Old Norse ves heill, 'be in good health', and in cider counties the bowl is still carried into the orchards in January to toast the trees themselves.

steps: Core the apples, fill them with brown sugar and roast at 180°C until soft and foaming, about 40 minutes.
Warm the ale and sherry with the spices and remaining sugar — steaming, never boiling.
Float the roasted apples in the bowl; the pulp bursting into the ale is where 'lamb's wool' gets its name.
Ladle into cups, making sure everyone gets some apple.
Serve hot, and pass the bowl rather than pouring individual drinks.

name: Smoking Bishop
description: Port and roasted oranges mulled together — the drink Scrooge promises Bob Cratchit on the last page of A Christmas Carol.
funFact: Dickens gave it the last line of dialogue in A Christmas Carol — 'a bowl of Smoking Bishop' — and the drink was already old enough by 1843 that he needed no footnote.

steps: Stud each orange with five cloves and roast at 180°C until browned, about an hour.
Quarter the roasted oranges and steep them in the red wine with the sugar and spices overnight.
Strain, pressing the fruit, then add the port.
Heat gently to steaming — never boil, or the port turns harsh.
Ladle into mugs and serve hot.

name: Lamb's Wool
description: Hot ale poured over roasted apple pulp until it froths white — the froth is the wool, and the drink is medieval.
funFact: The name describes the appearance: burst roasted apple whipped into hot ale forms a woolly white foam, and the drink belongs to Twelfth Night rather than Christmas.

steps: Roast the apples whole at 180°C until they split and collapse, about 45 minutes.
Scoop out the pulp and beat it smooth with the sugar and spices.
Warm the ale to steaming, then whisk it into the apple pulp a little at a time.
Keep whisking until the surface turns white and woolly.
Serve hot in tankards.

name: Syllabub
description: Cream whipped with sweet wine, sugar and lemon until it holds its shape. Tudor England's dessert, eaten with a spoon.
funFact: The earliest version was made by milking a cow directly into a bowl of spiced wine, so the froth formed on impact — a technique that limits where you can make it.

steps: Steep the lemon zest and juice in the wine and sherry with the sugar for several hours.
Strain out the zest and stir until the sugar has fully dissolved.
Pour the cream in slowly while whisking, until it holds soft peaks.
Spoon into small glasses and chill for at least two hours.
Grate nutmeg over just before serving, with a spoon.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and lemon zest

name: Negus
description: Port with hot water, lemon, sugar and nutmeg. Served to children at Victorian parties, which says something about the era.
funFact: Named for Colonel Francis Negus, who reportedly diluted the port at a heated gathering to calm the argument down; Dickens has it served at children's parties in more than one novel.

steps: Rub the sugar over the lemon zest to draw out the oil, then put both in a warmed jug.
Add the lemon juice and the port.
Pour in hot but not boiling water and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Ladle into warmed glasses.
Grate nutmeg over each serving.

name: Posset
description: Hot milk curdled deliberately with ale or wine, spiced and sweetened. Medicinal, medieval, and eaten as much as drunk.
funFact: Posset pots had a spout so the drinker could take the liquid from beneath while the curds sat on top; the modern lemon posset dessert kept the name and dropped the alcohol entirely.

steps: Warm the milk with the cinnamon and nutmeg until steaming; do not boil.
Warm the ale or wine separately with the sugar.
Pour the hot ale into the hot milk — it will curdle immediately, which is correct.
Let it stand a minute so the curd rises and the liquid settles below.
Serve hot, with a spoon.

name: Brandy Sour
description: Cyprus's national cocktail: local brandy, lemon squash, bitters and soda. Invented, by tradition, to disguise a king's drinking.
funFact: The story holds that it was created in the 1930s for King Farouk of Egypt, so a visiting Muslim monarch could be served something that looked like iced tea.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the brandy and lemon squash.
Dash the Angostura generously over the top.
Top with soda water and stir once.
Garnish with a lemon slice.

name: Kinnie and Gin
description: Malta's bitter-orange soda lengthening a measure of gin — wormwood and bitter orange over juniper.
funFact: Kinnie has been bottled in Malta since 1952 from bitter oranges and a mix of aromatic herbs including wormwood, and Maltese abroad have it shipped to them.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Pour in the gin.
Top with cold Kinnie.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice.

name: Rum and Raspberry
description: White rum with raspberry cordial and soda — 'R&R' across southern Africa, and a staple of Mozambican beach bars.
funFact: Ordered simply as 'R and R' from Maputo to Johannesburg, it is one of very few mixed drinks with genuine regional currency across southern Africa.

steps: Fill a tall glass with ice.
Add the rum, raspberry cordial and lime juice.
Top with cold soda water.
Stir once and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Fort Point
description: Rye, Punt e Mes, Bénédictine and maraschino — a Manhattan with the bitterness turned up and the sweetness pulled back.
funFact: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey; Punt e Mes is a vermouth with an extra measure of bitterness stirred in, and its name means 'point and a half' from an old Turin trading term.

steps: Stir all ingredients over ice for 25 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.
Serve cold.

name: Kentucky Maid
description: Bourbon with muddled cucumber and mint over lime. A Southside that went south, and better in summer than either parent.
funFact: Sam Ross built it at Milk & Honey as a bourbon answer to the gin Southside; cucumber and bourbon is an unlikely pairing that the mint holds together.

steps: Muddle two cucumber slices with the syrup in the shaker.
Add the mint and press once, gently.
Add the bourbon, lime juice and ice, then shake hard for 10 seconds.
Double-strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a cucumber slice and a mint sprig.

name: Death Flip
description: Tequila, yellow Chartreuse, Jägermeister and a whole egg. It should be undrinkable. It is one of the best modern cocktails made.
funFact: Chris Hysted created it at Black Pearl in Melbourne around 2010; the combination reads as a dare on paper and converts almost everyone who is talked into ordering one.

steps: Dry-shake all ingredients without ice for 20 seconds to build the texture.
Add ice and shake hard for another 15 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Grate nutmeg over the foam.
Serve immediately.

name: Gordon's Breakfast
description: Gin with lime, Worcestershire, Tabasco and muddled cucumber. A savoury gin sour that behaves like a Bloody Mary without the tomato.
funFact: Sam Ross named it for Gordon's gin and for the fact that it is, structurally, a breakfast drink — savoury, saline and built to be drunk before noon.

steps: Muddle the cucumber slices in the bottom of the shaker.
Add the gin, lime, syrup, Worcestershire, Tabasco and seasoning.
Add ice and shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a cucumber slice and a crack of black pepper.
